newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokai Kogyo files for protection, debt 511 bln yen.
newsitem.headline: Tokai Kogyo files for protection, debt 511 bln yen.

text.p: Japanese general contractor Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd said on Friday that it has filed for court protection from creditors and has debts of 511 billion yen.

Company president Kunihide Kobayashi told a news conference that the firm had obtained guarantees for further financial assistance from its four main banks -- Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd, Tokai Bank Ltd, the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan, and Norinchukin Bank -- to maintain its operations for now.
"I have decided on the move (court protection) because the company's business continued to decline while being unable to reduce debt," he said.
He also said that a possible rise in Japanese interest rates would put the company into deeper trouble.
Kobayashi also said that most of the company's top executives would resign to take responsibility for the company's business woes.
"We have been seeking up until the last minute to rebuild our business without seeking court protection. But we were forced to seek reorganisation under the legal process."

Tokai Kogyo is the first listed contractor to fail in the nation's post-war history. The last major failure of a Japanese general contractor was in 1993, when Osaka-based Muramoto Construction Co Ltd went under with debts of 530 billion yen.
Kobayashi said that a further decline in real estate prices and rising concerns about Tokai Kogyo's financial credibility forced it to abort its initial restructuring plan.

In November 1993, Tokai drafted a plan to rebuild its faltering business. This involved streamlining its operations, selling real estate holdings and asking creditor banks to lower interest rates on loans.
Tokai said its business deteriorated after the bursting of Japan's late-1980's "bubble" of inflated asset prices, which resulted in hefty borrowings and soaring interest rate payments.
But a continued worsening of the real estate market and dwindling profits from its mainstream construction business made it difficult to recover.

The firm said it had tried to draft another business rehabilitation plan. But with little sign of an upturn in its financial condition, and with the risk of higher interest rates, Tokai Kogyo said it had come to the decision that making further efforts to rebuild its business by itself would only trouble other companies.
"It was a painful choice, but we have decided to try to rebuild our business with the help of court assistance," the company said in the statement.
The company said it would try to complete ongoing construction projects under court instruction and with the help of related financial firms and other firms.
It said it would strive to rebuild its business in order to regain public trust.
